stages.title: Les bases
stages.can: Greet people, ask for what you need, and follow slow, simple speech about everyday things.
stages.why: The 350 commonest words cover about two thirds of everything said in French. They are mostly short, mostly irregular, and mostly the same in Québec and in France.

stages.title: Le quotidien
stages.can: Shop, travel, order a meal and make small talk; say what you did yesterday.
stages.why: Past time arrives here, because small talk is mostly about what just happened. This is also where Québec starts to sound different: the meals change names, and a dépanneur appears.

stages.title: Se débrouiller
stages.can: Get through an unplanned conversation about home, work, family and plans.
stages.why: The imperfect lets you describe how things were, and the little pronouns y and en stop your sentences sounding like a phrasebook.

stages.title: Raconter
stages.can: Tell a story with a beginning, a middle and a reason; say what you used to do and what you would do.
stages.why: Telling a story means holding two past tenses against each other, and the future and conditional let you step out of the past again.

stages.title: Donner son avis
stages.can: Agree, disagree and say why; follow a radio programme and most of a film.
stages.why: Opinion is where the subjunctive begins: "il faut que", "je veux que". It is the thing English speakers most often avoid, and most often get away with avoiding, until a conversation turns serious.

stages.title: Nuancer
stages.can: Hedge, qualify and concede; read a news article with only an occasional lookup.
stages.why: Words at this size are rarer, longer and more often abstract. Most are cognates with English — which helps, and is also where the false friends live.

stages.title: Lire la presse
stages.can: Read an editorial or a long report and follow the argument.
stages.why: Written French diverges from spoken French here: the vocabulary is the vocabulary of print.

stages.title: Aisance
stages.can: Understand nearly everything, including the literary and the formal, and notice register.
stages.why: The last thousand words in this list are the ones a well-read adult would recognise and a learner often will not.

conjLadder.title: Le présent : les douze essentiels
conjLadder.why: être, avoir, aller, faire and eight more. Nearly every sentence you say uses one of them, and all twelve are irregular, so they have to be known by heart.
conjLadder.uses: Nothing yet: this is the first block. Everything else stands on être and avoir.

teach.what: The present tense says what is true now, what is happening, and what happens regularly: je suis, tu as, nous allons. These twelve verbs are in almost every sentence.
teach.build: There is no rule for these: all twelve are irregular, so each of the six forms has to be known. Start with être (to be) and avoir (to have). They are also the two helpers that build the past tense.
teach.watch: Many have two stems, one for je / tu / il / ils and another for nous / vous: je veux, nous voulons; je peux, nous pouvons; je viens, nous venons. The nous and vous forms usually look more like the infinitive.

conjLadder.title: Le présent : les verbes en -er
conjLadder.why: Nine out of ten French verbs follow this one pattern. Learn it once and it covers parler, aimer, chercher, trouver and hundreds more.
conjLadder.uses: The six-person frame (je, tu, il, nous, vous, ils) that you met with the twelve essentials.

teach.what: Most French verbs end in -er, and they all follow one pattern in the present tense: parler, aimer, chercher, trouver, regarder and hundreds more.
teach.watch: Four of the six forms sound identical (je parle, tu parles, il parle, ils parlent). Only nous and vous sound different, so the spelling is where the work is. A few have spelling changes: manger → nous mangeons, acheter → j’achète, appeler → j’appelle.

conjLadder.title: Le présent : les autres verbes courants
conjLadder.en: Present tense: the other common verbs
conjLadder.why: The -ir and -re verbs and the irregulars. Each has a stem that changes (prends / prenons / prennent), which is why they are asked in several persons.
conjLadder.uses: The regular pattern, so you can see exactly where these verbs break it.

teach.what: The other common verbs end in -ir or -re, or are irregular outright. It is the same present tense, but there is no single pattern to lean on.
teach.build: The regular -ir verbs (finir, choisir) add -iss- in the plural: je finis, nous finissons. Regular -re verbs (vendre, attendre) lose the ending: je vends, nous vendons. Many common ones change stem: je prends, nous prenons, ils prennent.
teach.watch: Look at the stem in the nous form and in the ils form. The change usually happens between them: je veux / nous voulons / ils veulent.

conjLadder.title: Le passé composé
conjLadder.en: The past tense (“I have spoken”, “I spoke”)
conjLadder.why: The everyday past: a helper (avoir, or être for a few verbs of movement) plus the participle. Most of the work is knowing which helper, and the participle.
conjLadder.uses: The present of avoir and être (the helper), and the -er pattern, whose participle ends in -é.

teach.what: The everyday past tense. It means both “I spoke” and “I have spoken”: j’ai parlé.
teach.build: A helper in the present (avoir, for most verbs) plus the past participle. The participle of an -er verb ends in -é (parlé), of an -ir verb in -i (fini), of a regular -re verb in -u (vendu). Many common verbs have irregular participles, listed below.
teach.watch: A small group of verbs of movement and change use être as the helper instead: aller, venir, arriver, partir, rester, tomber, naître, mourir, devenir, revenir, entrer. With être the participle agrees with the subject: il est allé, elle est allée, ils sont allés, elles sont allées.

conjLadder.title: L’imparfait
conjLadder.en: The imperfect (“I was speaking”, “I used to speak”)
conjLadder.why: How things were. It is built from the “nous” form of the present, so once you know that, it is nearly regular.
conjLadder.uses: The nous form of the present: the imperfect is built from it.

teach.what: The imperfect describes how things were, what used to happen, and the background to a story: il pleuvait (it was raining), nous habitions à Montréal (we used to live in Montréal).
teach.build: Take the nous form of the present, drop -ons, and add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Nous parlons → je parlais. The only verb that does not work this way is être (j’étais).
teach.watch: The je and tu forms sound the same, and so do il and ils (parlait, parlaient). It is the tense for “was doing” and “used to”; the passé composé is for what happened once.

conjLadder.title: Le présent : plus de verbes
conjLadder.why: The same tense, now across the next several hundred verbs, including the ones with spelling changes (appeler → j’appelle, acheter → j’achète).
conjLadder.uses: Both present-tense patterns, now with spelling changes.

teach.what: The same present tense across the next several hundred verbs, including the ones that change their spelling to keep their sound.
teach.build: The patterns you already know still apply. What is new is the spelling change in the stem: acheter → j’achète, appeler → j’appelle, payer → je paie, manger → nous mangeons, commencer → nous commençons.
teach.watch: The change follows the sound: the stem is adjusted in je / tu / il / ils, while nous and vous keep the infinitive’s stem.

conjLadder.title: Le futur proche
conjLadder.en: The near future (“I’m going to speak”)
conjLadder.why: aller + the infinitive. It is how people actually talk about what is next, in Québec most of all.
conjLadder.uses: The present of aller, which you already know.

teach.what: The near future: what is about to happen or what you plan to do. Je vais parler, tu vas manger.
teach.build: The present tense of aller (shown below) plus the infinitive. Nothing else changes: the infinitive stays as it is.
teach.watch: It is how people usually talk about the future out loud, and more so in Québec. The simple future (next step) is used more in writing.

conjLadder.title: Le futur simple
conjLadder.why: The infinitive plus endings, with a handful of irregular stems (ir-, ser-, aur-, fer-, ver-).
conjLadder.uses: The infinitive and the present-tense patterns: the future is built on the infinitive.

teach.what: The simple future: je parlerai (I will speak).
teach.build: The infinitive plus -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont. A -re verb drops its final e first: vendre → je vendrai.
teach.watch: About a dozen common verbs have an irregular stem (their future forms are listed below), but the endings are always the same. The stem is what you have to learn.

conjLadder.title: Le conditionnel
conjLadder.why: The future’s stem with the imperfect’s endings. It is also the polite form: je voudrais, pourriez-vous.
conjLadder.uses: The future’s stem and the imperfect’s endings, both taught earlier.

teach.what: The conditional: what would happen, and the polite way to ask. Je parlerais (I would speak); je voudrais un café (I would like a coffee).
teach.build: The same stem as the future (parler-, ser-, aur-, ir-…) plus the imperfect’s endings: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.
teach.watch: If you know the future stem you know the conditional stem. The only difference between je parlerai and je parlerais is the ending.

conjLadder.title: L’impératif
conjLadder.why: Orders and invitations: parle, parlons, parlez. Mostly the present with the subject dropped; the -er verbs lose the s of “tu”.
conjLadder.uses: The tu, nous and vous forms of the present.

teach.what: The imperative gives orders, advice and invitations: parle ! parlons ! parlez !
teach.build: Take the tu, nous and vous forms of the present and drop the pronoun. Tu parles → parle ! Nous parlons → parlons ! Vous parlez → parlez !
teach.watch: An -er verb (and aller, ouvrir, offrir…) loses the final s of tu: tu parles → parle, but tu finis → finis. Three verbs are irregular: être → sois, soyons, soyez; avoir → aie, ayons, ayez; savoir → sache, sachons, sachez.

conjLadder.title: Le passé composé : plus de verbes
conjLadder.why: Irregular participles (pris, fait, vu, dit, mis, venu) are the part that has to be learnt one by one.
conjLadder.uses: The same build, with more participles.

teach.what: More verbs in the past tense. The build is the one you know; what is new is learning the participles that do not end in -é, -i or -u.
teach.build: Helper + participle, as before. The irregular participles are the part that has to be learnt one by one. The ones listed below cover a large share of everything you will say in the past.
teach.watch: Look for families: mettre / permettre / promettre all give -mis; prendre / comprendre / apprendre all give -pris.

conjLadder.title: Le plus-que-parfait
conjLadder.en: The past before the past (“I had spoken”)
conjLadder.why: The imperfect of avoir or être plus the participle: what had already happened when something else did.
conjLadder.uses: The imperfect (for the helper) and the participle you learnt for the passé composé.

teach.what: The pluperfect: the past before another past. J’avais parlé (I had spoken).
teach.build: The imperfect of the helper (avais, avais, avait, avions, aviez, avaient, or étais… for the être verbs) plus the past participle.
teach.watch: It shows which of two past events came first: the one in the pluperfect happened earlier. The participle is the same one you used in the passé composé.

conjLadder.title: Le subjonctif présent
conjLadder.why: After il faut que, je veux que, bien que. Regular verbs look like the present, so the work is in the irregular ones (que je sois, que j’aie, que je fasse).
conjLadder.uses: The ils form of the present, and the imperfect’s nous and vous forms.

teach.what: The subjunctive follows expressions of need, wish, doubt and feeling: il faut que tu parles, je veux qu’il vienne, bien qu’elle soit partie.
teach.build: For most verbs, take the ils form of the present, drop -ent, and add -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent. Ils parlent → que je parle. Nous and vous use the imperfect’s forms (que nous parlions).
teach.watch: For regular -er verbs it looks just like the present, so you cannot see it. It shows in the irregular ones, listed below. It always comes after que.

conjLadder.title: Le conditionnel passé et le futur antérieur
conjLadder.en: The conditional perfect and the future perfect
conjLadder.why: “I would have spoken” and “I will have spoken”: the same two-part build as the passé composé, with the helper in a different tense.
conjLadder.uses: The passé composé build, with the helper in the conditional or the future.

teach.what: Two more compound tenses. The conditional perfect: j’aurais parlé (I would have spoken). The future perfect: j’aurai parlé (I will have spoken).
teach.build: The same two-part build as the passé composé, with the helper in a different tense: the conditional or the future of avoir or être.
teach.watch: The participle never changes. Only the helper does, so these are mostly a matter of knowing the helper’s conditional and future forms.

conjLadder.title: Le subjonctif passé
conjLadder.en: The past subjunctive (“that I have spoken”)
conjLadder.why: The subjunctive of avoir or être plus the participle, for what has already happened: bien qu’il soit parti.
conjLadder.uses: The subjunctive of the helper and the participle.

teach.what: The past subjunctive: the subjunctive for something that has already happened. Bien qu’il ait parlé (although he has spoken).
teach.build: The subjunctive of the helper (aie, aies, ait, ayons, ayez, aient, or sois, sois, soit… for être verbs) plus the past participle.
teach.watch: It is used where the present subjunctive would be, but the action is finished. It is mostly met in writing and careful speech.

conjLadder.title: Les verbes moins courants, tous les temps
conjLadder.en: The less common verbs, in every tense
conjLadder.why: The long tail: every verb up to the 3,500th most frequent word, in two of the six main tenses each (a different two for each verb), one person at a time.
conjLadder.uses: Everything: this step is the whole ladder, applied to rarer verbs.

teach.what: The long tail: every verb up to the 3,500th most frequent word, in two tenses each.
teach.build: Nothing new here: the patterns, stems and participles of the earlier steps apply. When a verb is irregular, the answer the app shows you afterwards is the lesson.
teach.watch: These are rarer verbs, so treat wrong answers as the point: each one comes back on a later day with the full pattern shown.

expressions.note: Bol was borrowed from English “bowl” in the 18th century, so its first meaning is the dish: un bol de lait. Its second, informal meaning is luck. Wiktionary points to pot as the model: pot is a jar and also, informally, luck (avoir du pot). So bol most likely followed pot. Neither source says why a container came to mean luck, so there is no tidy story to tell: learn avoir du bol as one unit.
The same idea as avoir du bol, and the older of the two. Pot is a jar; informally it is also luck. You will also hear avoir de la chance, which is the ordinary, neutral way to say it.

expressions.en: to feel down, to have the blues
expressions.note: A cafard is a cockroach, and informally it is also a low, gloomy mood. The image is of something creeping and dark getting hold of you. Wiktionary gives the mood as a meaning of the word; it does not give a settled reason for the cockroach.

expressions.en: to not feel like doing something, to feel lazy
expressions.note: Flemme is informal laziness. J’ai la flemme de cuisiner means “I can’t be bothered to cook”: the word is followed by de + a verb.

ex.t: J'ai la flemme de le faire.
ex.e: I can't be bothered to do it.

expressions.en: to be full of energy, to be in great form
expressions.note: A fixed phrase: the peach stands for health and a rosy, lively look. As with most idioms, the sources give the meaning rather than a documented origin, so treat the explanation as the picture it paints, not as history.

You say it of someone who does not turn up to a meeting, a date or an appointment: Il m’a posé un lapin. The rabbit does not help you guess the meaning, and the sources do not settle where the phrase comes from, so learn it whole.

expressions.en: to tell tall tales, to talk nonsense
expressions.note: Besides the vegetable, salade is informal for nonsense, and is used in the plural: des salades. Wiktionary gives the meaning but not a settled reason; the usual picture is a jumble of ingredients tossed together, which is only a guess at why.
Navet is a turnip, a plain, unglamorous vegetable, and informally a film or other work that is poor. C’est un navet: “it’s a dud”.

ex.t: Au secours, seigneurs, au secours ! venez à l’aide de mon seigneur, qui est engagé dans la plus formidable et la plus sanglante bataille que mes yeux aient jamais vue. Vive Dieu ! il a porté un tel revers au géant ennemi de madame la princesse Micomicona, qu’il lui a tranché la tête à rasibus des épaules, comme si c’eût été un navet.
ex.e: Help, good sirs, help! Come to the help of my master, who is engaged in the most formidable and the most bloody battle that my eyes have ever seen. By God! He delivered such a backhand to the giant enemy of the lady princess of Micomicona that he sliced off his head cleanly from the shoulders, as if it had been a turnip.

expressions.note: A fixed phrase with no obvious link between apples and fainting; the sources give the meaning, not a settled origin. Just use it as one block: Elle est tombée dans les pommes.

expressions.en: to be kept waiting, to hang around
expressions.note: It is a verb made from poireau (leek), informal for waiting around, as if you were standing rooted in the ground like a leek. Wiktionary gives the meaning; the picture is the usual explanation, not a documented history.

ex.e: He left me hanging for 4 days.

expressions.note: Marcher is “to walk”, but also “to work” (a machine, a plan). Ça marche is the everyday way to agree: “works for me”, “deal”. It is also a question: Ça marche ? = “is that OK?”.
Faucher is to mow or cut down with a scythe, so fauché is literally “cut down”: someone whose money has been taken away. The informal “broke” meaning is listed as its own sense of the word.
Setting sail is how a ship departs, so the phrase is “to be off”. Here the picture and the meaning line up, which makes it one of the easier ones to remember.

ex.t: On est des étoiles dans ce ciel bleu clair et on mettra les voiles quand on pourra le faire.

expressions.en: to annoy someone, to be a pain
expressions.note: Informal and a little strong. Tu me casses les pieds ! = “you’re getting on my nerves”. Someone annoying is un casse-pieds.

ex.t: Tu me casses les pieds à tourner en rond depuis tout à l'heure !
ex.e: You're driving me crazy going around in circles this whole time!

expressions.literal: to give one’s tongue to the cat
expressions.note: Said when you give up trying to guess a riddle or a surprise: Je donne ma langue au chat. The cat has no connection to the meaning that the sources record, so learn it as one unit.

ex.t:
– Eh bien non, je ne vois pas.
– Vous donnez votre langue au chat alors, un seul mot pourtant.
– Oui c'est ça si vous voulez. Je donne ma langue au chat.
ex.e:
"No, I don't get it."
"You give up then? It's only one word, though."
"Yes, I do. I give up."

expressions.fr: coûter les yeux de la tête
expressions.literal: to cost the eyes of the head
expressions.note: The English phrase is “to cost an arm and a leg”: both name body parts you could not do without. Ça coûte les yeux de la tête.

ex.t: J'en ai marre de payer un loyer dans cette ville. Ça me coûte les yeux de la tête !
ex.e: I'm sick of paying rent in this town. It's costing me an arm and a leg!

expressions.fr: avoir le cœur sur la main
expressions.en: to be generous, to be open-hearted
expressions.literal: to have the heart on the hand
expressions.note: The heart is held out in the open hand, ready to be given. It is a compliment, not a criticism.

ex.t: Magali a le cœur sur la main.

expressions.en: to butt in, to put in one’s two cents
expressions.literal: to put in one’s grain of salt
expressions.note: Said of someone who adds an opinion nobody asked for. A grain of salt is tiny, but it flavours the whole dish, even when it was not wanted.
Same meaning as the English: avoiding the point instead of getting to it. Ne tourne pas autour du pot ! = “just say it”.

expressions.en: to sleep in, to have a lie-in
expressions.note: Gras (feminine grasse) is “fat” and here means rich or generous: a “fat” morning is a long one in bed. Not at all impolite; it is the ordinary expression for sleeping in.

expressions.en: to have one’s head in the clouds
expressions.note: Said of someone distracted or daydreaming. French puts the head in the moon where English puts it in the clouds.

expressions.en: to fall in love at first sight
expressions.note: A coup de foudre is a bolt of lightning: sudden, total and impossible to ignore. It is used of love at first sight, and also of a sudden strong liking for a place or an object.
Plombs are the lead fuses that used to cut the power when a circuit overloaded. Blowing a fuse is how English says it too: the person overloaded and shut down or exploded. Il a pété les plombs.

ex.t: Fausse diversion, un jour tu pètes les plombs / Les plombs, certains chanceux en ont dans la cervelle
ex.e: False diversion, one day you blow your top / Some guys who are lucky get their heads blown off

spotlight.title: Du, de la: “some”
spotlight.text: Je cherche du lait: du (de la before a feminine noun) means “some”. Le lait would mean one particular milk you both already know. You will hear du, de la and des all the time in shops and restaurants.

best.en: Yes, I’m looking for some milk.
best.why: Du means “some”: you want milk, not one particular milk.

others.why: Correct French, but le lait points to one particular milk you both know about.
After je, use the present: cherche. The infinitive (chercher) does not change for the subject.

lines.fr: Là-bas, dans le frigo, au fond.
lines.en: Over there, in the fridge, at the back.

best.why: Ça coûte combien ? is the everyday way to ask a price.

others.why: Correct French, but he has just told you where it is.
Coûtes is the tu form: you would be asking the clerk what he costs. Ça coûte means “it costs”.

lines.fr: Quatre dollars cinquante. Vous voulez autre chose ?
lines.en: Four fifty. Would you like anything else?

best.why: C’est tout means “that’s all”: the usual way to finish an order.

others.why: Understood, but c’est fini sounds as if something has ended; for an order you say c’est tout.
Here tout is the singular “all”, so it is tout, not tous.

lines.en: You’re welcome! Have a good day.

spotlight.title: Je vais + infinitive: the near future
spotlight.text: Je vais prendre la poutine is how people actually order. It is aller (present) plus the infinitive, and nothing else changes. Je prendrai is correct, but sounds stiff in speech.

lines.fr: Bonsoir ! Une table pour combien de personnes ?
lines.en: Good evening! A table for how many people?

best.why: S’il vous plaît: polite, and vous is right for someone you do not know.

others.why: S’il te plaît is for someone you call tu. A server you don’t know gets s’il vous plaît.

others.fr: Pour deux personne, s’il vous plaît.
others.why: After deux the noun is plural: deux personnes (the s is silent, so it only shows in writing).

lines.fr: Suivez-moi. Vous voulez voir le menu du souper ?
lines.en: Follow me. Would you like to see the supper menu?

best.fr: Oui, merci. Qu’est-ce que vous me conseillez ?
best.en: Yes, thanks. What do you recommend?
best.why: Qu’est-ce que… is the everyday “what”; vous, as before.

others.fr: Oui, merci. Qu’est-ce que tu me conseilles ?
others.why: Correct, but tu is for a friend. A server is vous.

others.fr: Oui, merci. Que vous me conseillez ?
others.why: A spoken question like this needs qu’est-ce que (or que with inversion: Que me conseillez-vous ?).

lines.fr: La poutine est très bonne. Vous voulez boire quelque chose ?
lines.en: The poutine is very good. Would you like something to drink?

best.fr: Je vais prendre la poutine et une liqueur, s’il vous plaît.
best.en: I’ll have the poutine and a soft drink, please.
best.why: Je vais prendre is the everyday way to order, and une liqueur is a soft drink in Québec.

others.fr: Je prendrai la poutine et une liqueur, s’il vous plaît.
others.why: Correct (simple future) but stiff; in speech the near future is what people say.

others.fr: Je vais prendre la poutine et un liqueur, s’il vous plaît.
others.why: Liqueur is feminine: une liqueur.

spotlight.title: Tu or vous?
spotlight.text: With a neighbour of your own age, tu is the normal choice in Québec; vous would sound distant. With a server, a clerk or a stranger it is vous. The imperative viens! is the tu form of venir with the pronoun dropped.

best.why: A neighbour who says salut expects tu, so et toi.

others.why: Correct, but with a neighbour your age vous sounds distant.
Ton is “your” before a noun. “And you” is et toi.

lines.fr: Qu’est-ce que tu fais en fin de semaine ?
lines.en: What are you doing on the weekend?

best.fr: Je vais magasiner un peu. Et toi ?
best.en: I’m going to do some shopping. And you?
best.why: Magasiner is the Québec verb for going shopping, and je vais + infinitive for the plan.

others.fr: Je vais faire les courses un peu. Et toi ?
others.why: Correct French, but faire les courses is grocery shopping; magasiner is shopping around for things.

others.fr: Je vais magasine un peu. Et toi ?
others.why: After je vais use the infinitive: magasiner.

lines.fr: Moi, je vais au chalet. Viens au cinq à sept vendredi !
lines.en: Me, I’m going to the cottage. Come to the 5 to 7 on Friday!

best.en: With pleasure, shall I bring something?
best.why: Avec plaisir accepts warmly; j’apporte (present) offers to bring something.

others.why: Correct French, but it turns down a friendly invitation; the moment calls for a yes.
With je the present is j’apporte. The ending -a belongs to il / elle.

spotlight.title: Être in the passé composé
spotlight.text: Partir is one of the verbs of movement that use être, not avoir: le bus est parti. The participle agrees with the subject (elle est partie). Most verbs use avoir: il a mangé.

best.fr: Excusez-moi, le bus pour le centre-ville est déjà parti ?
best.en: Excuse me, has the downtown bus already left?
best.why: Partir takes être: est parti. And excusez-moi, because this is a stranger.

others.fr: Excuse-moi, le bus pour le centre-ville est déjà parti ?
others.why: Correct, but excuse-moi is tu. To a stranger: excusez-moi.

others.fr: Excusez-moi, le bus pour le centre-ville a déjà parti ?
others.why: Partir uses être in the passé composé: est parti, not a parti.

lines.fr: Oui, il est parti il y a cinq minutes. Le prochain arrive dans dix minutes.

best.fr: D’accord. Il passe par le centre-ville ?

others.why: Correct French, but nothing has been said about a light yet.

others.fr: D’accord. Il passer par le centre-ville ?
others.why: The subject il needs the present: passe, not the infinitive passer.

lines.fr: Oui. Descendez après la lumière, au deuxième arrêt.
lines.en: Yes. Get off after the traffic light, at the second stop.

best.why: Merci beaucoup: a plain, warm thank-you.

others.why: Bienvenue means “you’re welcome”, said after someone thanks YOU, not to thank them.

spotlight.title: En: “some of it, of them”
spotlight.text: En replaces “some of it / of them”, and goes before the verb: Prenez-en une = take one (of them). J’en prends une = I’m taking one. Also: pain is avoir mal à (j’ai mal à la gorge), and feelings with être (je suis fatigué).

lines.fr: Bonjour, qu’est-ce que je peux faire pour vous ?
lines.en: Hello, what can I do for you?

best.fr: J’ai mal à la gorge depuis hier.
best.en: I’ve had a sore throat since yesterday.
best.why: Avoir mal à + the body part is how French says it hurts.

others.fr: J’ai mal dans la gorge depuis hier.
others.why: Understood, but the usual form is avoir mal à: j’ai mal à la gorge.

others.fr: Je suis mal à la gorge depuis hier.
others.why: Pain uses avoir (j’ai mal à), not être.

best.fr: Non, mais je suis très fatigué.
best.why: Je suis fatigué: how you feel uses être. (Fatiguée if you are a woman.)

others.fr: Non, mais j’ai de la fièvre.
others.why: Correct French, but it says the opposite of what you mean: he asked about a fever.
How you feel uses être: je suis fatigué, not j’ai.

lines.fr: Prenez-en une toutes les quatre heures.

best.why: En stands for “of them” and goes before the verb: j’en prends une.

others.why: Correct French, but it means “I’m taking them (all)”, not one.
A pronoun for “of them” is en, and it goes before the verb: j’en prends.

grammar.title: Un or une
grammar.plain: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, and nothing about the thing itself tells you which. Masculine nouns take un or le; feminine nouns take une or la. Endings help — and the app measures how well on its own word list, so you can see how far to trust them.
grammar.watch: English gives you no warning, so the only safe habit is to learn the noun with its article: une maison, un chat, never just maison.

grammar.title: Être, avoir, aller, faire
grammar.plain: Être (to be) and avoir (to have) are the two verbs everything else leans on. They are irregular, they are the commonest words in the language, and they are the helpers that build the past. Aller (to go) and faire (to do, to make) are nearly as irregular and nearly as common.
grammar.watch: In speech, tu es shrinks to t’es, and in Québec je suis is often heard as chu — chu fatigué. Both are normal, and neither is written in a letter.

grammar.title: The -er verbs
grammar.plain: Most French verbs end in -er and follow one pattern: drop the -er and add -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent. Parler: je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent.
grammar.watch: Four of those six forms sound identical. Only nous and vous are audibly different, so the spelling — the part that is silent — is what fades first.

grammar.title: The everyday past
grammar.plain: The passé composé is a helper plus a past participle. Most verbs take avoir: j’ai mangé. About a dozen verbs of movement or change take être — aller, venir, arriver, partir, rester, tomber, mourir and their compounds — and so does every reflexive verb: elle est allée.
grammar.watch: English “I have eaten” and “I ate” both become j’ai mangé. And when the helper is être the participle agrees with the subject, which English never makes you do.

grammar.title: The irregular verbs
grammar.plain: Prendre, venir, pouvoir, vouloir, devoir, savoir, dire, voir and mettre each break the pattern in their own way, and each is worth knowing as a set of six. They are the verbs that carry a conversation.
grammar.watch: Pouvoir and vouloir share a shape (je peux, je veux), and prendre gives you comprendre and apprendre for free: learn one and you have several.

grammar.title: Ne … pas
grammar.plain: French negation wraps the verb: the ne goes before it and the pas after. Je ne sais pas. The other negatives take the same two slots: ne … jamais (never), ne … rien (nothing), ne … plus (no longer), ne … personne (nobody).
grammar.watch: In speech the ne is almost always dropped — je sais pas, and often j’sais pas — in Québec as in France. In writing, dropping it makes you look careless.

grammar.title: Words that sound the same (1)
grammar.plain: Many French words sound identical and differ only in spelling. The pairs that catch everyone: a (has) and à (to, at); ou (or) and où (where); et (and) and est (is); son (his, her) and sont (are); on (one, we) and ont (have).
grammar.watch: Swap-test: if you can replace it with avait it is a; with était it is est; with étaient it is sont; with avaient it is ont; with ou bien it is ou.

grammar.title: How things were
grammar.plain: The imperfect describes how things were, what used to happen, or what was going on when something else interrupted. Take the nous form of the present, drop -ons, and add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient: nous parlons gives je parlais. Être is the one exception: j’étais.
grammar.watch: English needs “used to” or “was …-ing”; French has no separate forms for either. Je mangeais means both. Three of the endings sound identical, so it is the written ending that decides.

grammar.title: The near future
grammar.plain: The near future is aller in the present plus an infinitive: je vais manger, nous allons partir. It is how French speakers actually talk about what is coming, from a minute away to next year.
grammar.watch: It is the spoken default. The simple future — je mangerai — is rarer in conversation and more formal.

examples.e: Go and see who it is.

examples.t: Je suis sûr qu'ils vont gagner.

grammar.title: Little pronouns
grammar.plain: Object pronouns come before the verb, not after: je le vois (I see him), il lui parle (he is talking to her), nous y allons (we are going there), j’en veux (I want some). Le, la and les stand in for a person or thing; lui and leur for “to someone”; y for “to or at a place”; en for “some of it” or “of it”.
grammar.watch: The pronoun jumps in front of the verb, which feels backwards to an English speaker. With a negative it sits inside the ne … pas: je ne le vois pas.

grammar.title: Words that sound the same (2)
grammar.plain: More pairs that sound alike. Ces (these) and ses (his, her); c’est (it is) and s’est (himself/herself, with a past verb); ce (this) and se (himself, herself); mais (but) and mes (my); peu (little), peut and peux (can); sur (on) and sûr (sure).
grammar.watch: Ask what the word is doing. A pronoun before a verb is se; a pointing word before a noun is ce; a possessive is ses or mes.

grammar.title: The simple future
grammar.plain: The simple future is the infinitive plus -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont: je parlerai, nous finirons. A short list of verbs have irregular stems — aller (ir-), être (ser-), avoir (aur-), faire (fer-), pouvoir (pourr-), voir (verr-) — but the endings never change.
grammar.watch: The endings are avoir in the present, which is no accident: parler + ai became parlerai.

grammar.title: What would happen
grammar.plain: The conditional takes the future stem and the imperfect endings: je parlerais, nous finirions. It softens requests — je voudrais — and says what would happen if something were true.
grammar.watch: “Je veux un café” is blunt; “je voudrais un café” is how you ask. After si in the same sentence, the si-clause takes the imperfect, never the conditional: si j’avais le temps, je viendrais.

grammar.title: When the participle agrees
grammar.plain: With être as the helper, the past participle agrees with the subject like an adjective: add -e for feminine, -s for plural. Il est allé, elle est allée, ils sont allés, elles sont allées. With avoir, the participle normally stays put.
grammar.watch: None of it is audible: allé, allée, allés and allées sound the same. It is a purely written skill, which is exactly why it fades.

grammar.title: Qui, que, dont, où
grammar.plain: Relative pronouns join clauses. Qui replaces a subject (la femme qui parle), que a direct object (le livre que je lis), dont something introduced by de (le livre dont je parle), and où a place or a time (la ville où j’habite).
grammar.watch: English often drops the pronoun — “the book I read” — and French never does: le livre que j’ai lu.

examples.e: Do you know who I am?

examples.t: Je sais que vous êtes riche.
Je sais que tu es riche.

grammar.title: The subjunctive
grammar.plain: The subjunctive follows expressions of wish, necessity, doubt and feeling, joined by que: il faut que tu viennes, je veux qu’il parte, bien qu’elle soit fatiguée. For most -er verbs it looks like the present indicative, so it only shows in the irregular ones: que je sois, que j’aie, que je fasse, que je puisse, que j’aille.
grammar.watch: It is the form English speakers avoid most and notice least. “Il faut que je vais” is the classic slip: after il faut que, the verb is subjunctive.

notes.title: Actuellement is not “actually”
notes.plain: Actuellement means “at the moment” or “currently”. For “actually”, French says en fait, or uses vraiment.
notes.watch: It is among the most common slips of English speakers writing French, and it stays in the sentence unnoticed because it looks right.

notes.title: Assister à is “to attend”
notes.plain: Assister à une réunion is to attend a meeting. It is not “to assist”: for that, French says aider.
notes.watch: And attendre, which looks as though it should mean “to attend”, means “to wait for”.

notes.title: Attendre is “to wait”
notes.plain: Attendre means to wait for. J’attends le bus: I am waiting for the bus. The word does not take a preposition for “for”.
notes.watch: It also sits close to entendre (to hear) on the page, and the two are mistaken for each other in fast reading.

notes.title: Déception is “disappointment”
notes.plain: A déception is a disappointment. French for “deception” is tromperie, and for “to deceive” it is tromper.
notes.watch: The verb is décevoir, to disappoint.

notes.title: Demander is “to ask”, not “to demand”
notes.plain: Demander means to ask, politely and neutrally: je lui ai demandé de venir. To demand, French says exiger.
notes.watch: Using demander where English has “demand” makes you sound far softer than you mean to be.

notes.title: Librairie is a bookshop
notes.plain: A librairie sells books. A bibliothèque is where you borrow them: a library.
notes.watch: A bibliothèque is also a bookcase.

notes.title: Location is “renting”
notes.plain: Location is the act of renting something: une voiture de location, a rental car. For the place where something is, French says lieu or endroit.
notes.watch: On a real-estate sign in Québec, à louer and à vendre are the pair: to rent and to sell.

notes.title: Sensible is “sensitive”
notes.plain: Sensible means sensitive or easily affected, not sensible. For “sensible, reasonable”, French says raisonnable.
notes.watch: Un enfant sensible is a sensitive child, not a sensible one.

notes.title: Supporter is “to put up with”
notes.plain: Supporter means to bear or tolerate: je ne supporte pas le bruit. To support someone — to back them — French says soutenir.
notes.watch: Un supporter is also a fan of a team. For backing someone’s idea or decision, soutenir is the careful choice.

notes.title: Conférence is a talk
notes.plain: A conférence is a lecture or a talk given to an audience, and also a conference. Lecture is not a lecture: it means reading.
notes.watch: It is lecture, with the same shape, that English speakers reach for.

notes.title: Réunion is a meeting
notes.plain: Une réunion is a meeting. A “reunion” of old friends is des retrouvailles.
notes.watch: It is also the name of an island in the Indian Ocean.

notes.title: Délai is a time limit
notes.plain: Un délai is the time allowed for something: dans un délai de trois jours, within three days. A delay — being late — is un retard.
notes.watch: Respecter les délais is to meet the deadlines.

notes.title: Un stage is an internship
notes.plain: Un stage is a work placement or a training course: faire un stage, to do an internship. The stage of a theatre is la scène.
notes.watch: A stagiaire is the intern.

notes.title: Large is “wide”
notes.plain: Large means wide. Something big overall is grand or gros; something wide is large: une rue large.
notes.watch: Il est large d’épaules is broad-shouldered, and has nothing to do with being large in general.

notes.title: Grand and gros
notes.plain: Grand is big in height or importance, and is what you say about a tall person. Gros is big in girth: thick, heavy, fat. A grand arbre is a tall tree; un gros arbre is a thick one.
notes.watch: Say gros about a person and it is about weight, so choose carefully.

notes.title: Ancien before and after the noun
notes.plain: Before a noun, ancien means “former”: mon ancien patron, my former boss. After a noun it means “ancient” or “old”: une ville ancienne. Vieux is “old” in the everyday sense.
notes.watch: The same adjective, two meanings, decided by where it sits.

notes.title: Formidable is “great”
notes.plain: Formidable means fantastic or tremendous. It has lost the sense of “fearsome” that English “formidable” keeps.
notes.watch: C’est formidable! is a compliment.

notes.title: Éventuel is “possible”
notes.plain: Éventuel means possible or potential: une éventuelle erreur, a possible mistake. It does not mean “eventual”: for that, French says final.
notes.watch: The adverb éventuellement means “possibly”. Wiktionary marks the sense “eventually” as Québec usage, so you will hear it both ways; “eventually” in France is finalement or un jour.

notes.title: Savoir and connaître
notes.plain: Both are “to know”. Savoir is to know a fact or a skill: je sais nager, je sais où il habite. Connaître is to be acquainted with a person, a place, a work: je connais Marie, je connais Montréal.
notes.watch: English uses one word for both, which is why this is one of the last things to settle.

notes.title: Bring and take: four words
notes.plain: French splits “bring” and “take” by whether it is a thing or a person, and which way it is going. Apporter: bring a thing here. Amener: bring a person here. Emporter: take a thing away. Emmener: take a person away.
notes.watch: The prefix gives it away: em- and en- mean away from here, a- means towards.

notes.title: Four ways to leave
notes.plain: Quitter takes an object: you quit a place or a person. Partir does not: je pars, I am leaving. Laisser is to leave something behind. Sortir is to go out.
notes.watch: Je quitte Montréal and je pars de Montréal are both right; je pars Montréal is not.

notes.title: Hear and listen, see and look
notes.plain: Entendre is to hear, which just happens. Écouter is to listen, which you do on purpose. Voir is to see; regarder is to look at, or to watch.
notes.watch: In Canadian French, écouter is also used for watching television: écouter un film.

notes.title: Going back
notes.plain: Rentrer is to go home, or back in. Retourner is to go back to a place. Revenir is to come back to where the speaker is.
notes.watch: Je rentre means “I am heading home”.

notes.title: Blesser is “to wound”
notes.plain: Blesser is to wound or injure; je suis blessé means I am hurt. It has nothing to do with blessing, which is bénir.
notes.watch: It also covers hurting someone’s feelings.

notes.title: Sympathique is “nice”
notes.plain: Sympathique describes someone friendly and likeable: elle est très sympathique. It is not “sympathetic” in the sense of feeling for someone’s trouble.
notes.watch: In speech it shrinks to sympa.

notes.title: Jour and journée, an and année
notes.plain: The short forms — jour, an, matin, soir — name a point or a unit: bonjour, deux ans, ce matin. The long forms — journée, année, matinée, soirée — name the span, with what happens in it: bonne journée, toute l’année, une soirée entre amis.
notes.watch: Bonne journée, not bon jour, as you leave a shop.

a-à.tip: Try avait: il avait mangé works, so it is a. Otherwise it is à.

ou-où.tip: Try ou bien (or else): if it fits, it is ou. If it asks about a place or a time, it is où.

et-est.tip: Try était: if il était fits, it is est. If it joins two things, it is et.

son-sont.tip: Try étaient: if ils étaient fits, it is sont. If it sits before a noun and means his or her, it is son.

on-ont.tip: Try avaient: if ils avaient fits, it is ont. If it means we or one, it is on.

ces-ses.tip: Ces points at things (these). Ses belongs to someone (his, her, its).

ce-se.tip: Se is a pronoun that sits right before a verb: il se lève. Ce points at something: ce livre.

mais-mes.tip: Mes is plural “my” and sits before a noun. Mais is “but” and joins two ideas.

peu-peut.tip: Peut is a verb (can). Peu is a quantity (little, few) and never changes.

sur-sûr.tip: Sûr, with its little hat, means sure. Sur, without, means on.

la-là.tip: Là, with the accent, is “there”. La is the, or her, and sits right before a noun or a verb.

du-dû.tip: Dû, with the little hat, is the participle of devoir (owed, had to). Du is “of the”.

leur-leurs.tip: Leur before a singular noun, leurs before a plural one. And leur before a verb never takes an s.

tout-tous.tip: Tous is plural (all of them). Tout is singular, or the adverb “quite”.
